Fish Washer.

I worked at a salmon processing plant in Alaska one summer. A forklift would put a tote of fish into a hopper that would feed a conveyor belt. The first guys (headers) would cut the heads off the fish. The next guys (slitters) would slit the belly, pull out the guts, cut down the blood line along the backbone, and if there were any eggs set them aside in baskets. Next were the spooners who would spoon out the globs of blood from the blood line. The next in line were the washers. There was a trough of freezing water between where you stood and the conveyor belt full of fish. You'd pull a fish into the trough, rinse off blood, pull off membranes and any guts left behind and put them back on the belt. The graders then sorted them by quality and weight. Then they went to either the freezer, fresh pack, or if they weren't of high enough quality for either of those two options, packed up for the cannery. Yeah...I don't eat canned salmon.

It was cold, wet, monotonous work. And happily, about a third of the way through the summer I was able to move down the line to be a grader.

The high wage and long hours wound up paying for my tuition that fall/spring. Many of my co-workers were there for the same reason.
